concepts.name: Constitutional Basis for State Legislature Structure
key_dimensions: Article 168: Composition of State Legislatures — Governor + Legislative Assembly (+ Legislative Council where applicable)
Distinction between states with bicameral vs unicameral legislatures under Part VI
Why the Constitution does not mandate uniformity — federal flexibility principle
Comparison with Parliament's mandatory bicameral structure under Article 79

concepts.name: Creation and Abolition of Legislative Council under Article 169
key_dimensions: Special majority requirement: resolution by Legislative Assembly by not less than 2/3 of members present and voting AND more than half of total membership
Parliament's role: Parliament passes an ordinary law (simple majority) — NOT a constitutional amendment under Article 368
UPSC Trap: Article 169 is an exception to Article 368 — Parliament can alter state legislature structure without state ratification
Recent controversy: Andhra Pradesh LC abolished (2020) and Jammu & Kashmir LC abolished (J&K Reorganisation Act 2019)
States currently having Legislative Councils: UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana (5 states as of 2024)

concepts.name: Composition and Strength of Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)
key_dimensions: Article 171: Total members not more than 1/3 of total Legislative Assembly members AND not less than 40 (minimum floor)
UPSC Trap: The 40-member minimum is absolute — the 1/3 cap is the maximum ceiling
J&K exception: LC was abolished; now only a unicameral UT with legislature
Comparison with Rajya Sabha composition logic (proportional vs fixed)

concepts.name: Composition Categories of Legislative Council — The 5/6ths Breakdown
key_dimensions: Article 171(3): 1/3 elected by local bodies, 1/12 by graduates (3+ years), 1/12 by teachers (secondary+), 1/3 elected by Legislative Assembly members, 1/6 nominated by Governor
UPSC Trap: Governor nominates 1/6 (not 1/12) — analogous to President's 12 nominees to Rajya Sabha but different fraction
Graduates' and Teachers' constituencies are unique to the LC — no parallel in Parliament
Distinction: Rajya Sabha members elected by elected MLAs only; LC has multiple electoral colleges

concepts.name: Governor's Nomination Power to Legislative Council
key_dimensions: Governor nominates 1/6 of total LC strength — persons with special knowledge/practical experience in literature, science, arts, cooperative movement, social service
UPSC Trap: The categories are different from President's Rajya Sabha nominees (art, literature, science, social service — NO cooperative movement for RS)
Discretionary vs ministerial aid: Whether Governor acts on CM's advice for nomination — constitutional convention vs practice
Controversy: Delay in nominations used as political tool (Maharashtra, Karnataka precedents)

concepts.name: Term, Tenure and Rotation of Legislative Council Members
key_dimensions: Article 172: LC is a permanent House — NOT subject to dissolution (parallel with Rajya Sabha)
Each member serves 6-year term; 1/3 retire every 2 years
UPSC Trap: Unlike Rajya Sabha where President notifies retirement batches, LC retirement schedule governed by Parliament-made law
Governor can extend term during national emergency (Article 172(1) proviso) — same as Rajya Sabha/Lok Sabha

concepts.name: Qualifications and Disqualifications for Legislative Council Membership
key_dimensions: Article 173: Minimum age 30 years for LC (vs 25 for Legislative Assembly) — UPSC frequently tests this
Must be enrolled voter in the state; must be a citizen of India
Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection): Applies equally to LC members as to LA members
Article 191 disqualifications: Office of profit, unsound mind, insolvent, not citizen — same as LA; no distinction

concepts.name: Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) — Composition and Strength
key_dimensions: Article 170: Not more than 500 and not less than 60 members — directly elected
UPSC Trap: Exceptions — Sikkim (32), Goa (40), Mizoram (40) have less than 60 by special constitutional provisions
Article 333: Governor may nominate ONE Anglo-Indian member (now lapsed after 104th Amendment, 2020)
Delimitation basis: Census figures — currently frozen on 1971 census until 2026 (Article 82/170)

concepts.name: Powers of Legislative Assembly vs Legislative Council — Financial Bills
key_dimensions: Money Bills (Article 198 + 207): Can only be introduced in Legislative Assembly; LC can delay for 14 days only — cannot amend or reject
UPSC Trap: LC recommendations on Money Bill can be accepted OR rejected by LA — LA's will prevails absolutely
Financial Bills (Category 1 & 2) — different treatment from Money Bills; Category 1 similar to Money Bill, Category 2 can be introduced in either House
Comparison with Rajya Sabha: Same subordinate position on Money Bills — 14 days delay power only

concepts.name: Deadlock Resolution Between Two Houses of State Legislature
key_dimensions: CRITICAL UPSC TRAP: There is NO provision for a Joint Sitting of the two Houses of a State Legislature (unlike Articles 108 for Parliament)
If LC rejects/delays a non-Money Bill: LA can pass it again; LC can delay for a maximum of 4 months total (3 months first + 1 month second detention) then LA's version prevails
This makes the LC a 'revising chamber' not a co-equal chamber — unlike Rajya Sabha's stronger position
Practical implication: LC cannot permanently block legislation — designed to be a check, not a veto

concepts.name: Ordinary Bill Passage in Bicameral State Legislature
key_dimensions: Article 197: Procedure if LC fails to pass, passes with amendments unacceptable to LA, or delays beyond 3 months
LA passes bill second time → sent to LC → if LC again rejects/delays beyond 1 month → deemed passed
Total maximum delay by LC: 3 months (first detention) + 1 month (second detention) = 4 months
UPSC Trap: For Rajya Sabha deadlock, Joint Sitting is called; for LC deadlock, LA alone prevails after prescribed delay — no joint sitting

concepts.name: Speaker and Chairman — Powers, Election and Removal
key_dimensions: Legislative Assembly: Speaker (Article 178) elected by LA members; Deputy Speaker also elected by LA
Legislative Council: Chairman elected by LC members; Deputy Chairman also elected by LC members
Removal: Speaker removed by effective majority (majority of ALL members) of LA with 14-day advance notice; same logic for Chairman of LC
UPSC Trap: During removal resolution, Speaker/Chairman does NOT preside — Deputy presides; BUT Speaker/Chairman can speak and vote in first instance (unlike normal casting vote rule)

concepts.name: Speaker's Role During Dissolution and Constitutional Conventions
key_dimensions: Article 179: Speaker vacates office if ceases to be member of LA; but does NOT vacate on dissolution — continues until new LA's first sitting
UPSC Trap: Speaker remains even after dissolution of LA — critical for continuity of office
Anti-Defection: Speaker/Chairman is the sole authority to decide disqualification under Tenth Schedule — judicial review available only after decision (Kihoto Hollohan case)
Casting vote: Speaker votes only in case of equality of votes (not an ordinary vote)

concepts.name: Quorum, Sessions and Summoning of State Legislature
key_dimensions: Article 174: Governor summons, prorogues and dissolves the Legislative Assembly (on CM's advice)
Quorum: 1/10th of total membership of each House (Article 189) — same ratio as Parliament
UPSC Trap: Maximum gap between two sessions — Article 174 says sessions must be held such that 6 months do not intervene between last sitting of one session and first sitting of next session
Governor cannot dissolve LC (permanent House) — can only dissolve LA; prorogation applies to both

concepts.name: Privileges of State Legislature — Articles 194 and 105 Analogy
key_dimensions: Article 194: Freedom of speech in state legislature; no court proceedings for anything said/voted in legislature
Members not liable to arrest in civil cases during session, 40 days before and after session
UPSC Trap: Article 194 mirrors Article 105 (Parliament) but courts have held that state legislatures cannot claim privileges beyond those of Parliament as of 1950 (until codified)
MSM Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (1959): Landmark case on legislative privilege vs fundamental rights — privilege can override Article 19(1)(a) in certain cases

concepts.name: Elected vs Nominated Members — Voting Rights in Presidential Election
key_dimensions: Article 54/55: Only ELECTED members of Legislative Assembly participate in Presidential election — NOT nominated members, NOT LC members
UPSC Trap: LC members (whether elected or nominated) do NOT participate in Presidential election
Vice Presidential election (Article 66): Elected by members of BOTH Houses of Parliament — state legislatures have NO role
Nominated MLA: Does not vote in Presidential election; nominated MLC: also excluded — double exclusion principle

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law and Its Application to State Legislatures
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule (added by 52nd Amendment 1985): Applies to both LA and LC members — voluntary surrender of party membership or voting against party whip triggers disqualification
Decision-making authority: Speaker (LA) and Chairman (LC) — their decision is final subject to judicial review
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): Supreme Court upheld Tenth Schedule; Speaker's decision is quasi-judicial; judicial review available AFTER decision, not during
UPSC Trap: Merger exception — at least 2/3 of party members must agree for it to count as merger (not split); original 'split' provision was deleted by 91st Amendment 2003

concepts.name: State Legislature vs Parliament — Legislative Competence and Overlaps
key_dimensions: Seventh Schedule: State List (List II) — 61 subjects exclusively for state legislatures; Concurrent List (List III) — Parliament prevails in case of repugnancy (Article 254)
Article 249: Parliament can legislate on State List if Rajya Sabha passes resolution by 2/3 majority (national interest) — state legislature's power temporarily superseded
Article 356 (President's Rule): State legislature's powers exercised by Parliament — Parliament can delegate to President; ordinances by President replace state ordinances
UPSC Trap: Under Article 252, if two or more states request Parliament to legislate on a State List subject, Parliament can do so — other states can adopt by resolution

concepts.name: Governor's Ordinance-Making Power and State Legislature
key_dimensions: Article 213: Governor issues ordinances when state legislature is not in session — must be approved by state legislature within 6 weeks of reassembly

UPSC Trap: Governor CANNOT promulgate ordinance without President's instructions in 3 cases: (1) if bill requires President's assent, (2) if Governor would have reserved bill for President, (3) if state legislature bill was declared invalid by President
Ordinance cannot override constitutional provisions or parliamentary laws on Concurrent/Union List
RC Cooper and DC Wadhwa cases: Ordinance raj (re-promulgation) condemned by Supreme Court — applies to state governors too

concepts.name: Reservation of State Bills for Presidential Assent — Article 200 and 201
key_dimensions: Article 200: Governor may assent, withhold assent, or reserve bill for President's consideration; can return non-Money Bills once for reconsideration
UPSC Trap: If LA passes bill again (with or without amendment), Governor MUST give assent — cannot withhold second time for ordinary bills; BUT for reserved bills, President is not so bound
Article 201: President may assent, withhold assent on reserved bills; if withheld, state legislature can reconsider but President is NOT obliged to give assent even then

Recent controversy: Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor (2023) ruled Governor cannot indefinitely withhold assent — must act within reasonable time; Article 200 uses 'shall'
